summary: Gateway-Initiated Dual-Stack Lite is a variant of DS-Lite for certain tunnel-based access networks. It extends existing access tunnels past the access gateway to an IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT using softwires with a Context Identifier to identify the end system.

eli5.summary: Instead of building a new tunnel for each home, this reuses existing tunnels and adds a name tag so the NAT knows who each packet belongs to.

questions: what is a context identifier in ds-lite
how does gateway-initiated ds-lite differ from ds-lite
subtitle: Reuse the tunnels an access network already has to reach a carrier NAT, tagging each device's traffic with a Context Identifier.

tldr.problem: Dual-Stack Lite normally builds a tunnel from each customer device to a carrier NAT, but tunnel-based access networks already have a tunnel from each device to an access gateway that serves large numbers of devices.
tldr.mechanism: The access gateway extends service to the carrier NAT (the AFTR) over a shared softwire, and a Context Identifier carried with each packet tells the AFTR which access device the traffic belongs to.
tldr.outcome: Service providers can share public IPv4 addresses among customers, even when devices use overlapping private IPv4 addresses, without changing the access device or the access architecture.

facts.label: Uniqueness rule
facts.value: CID and SWID unique between access gateway and AFTR

today: RFC 6674 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on DS-Lite as defined in RFC 6333.

sections.title: Overview and Motivation
sections.content:
Gateway-Initiated Dual-Stack Lite (GI-DS-Lite) is a variant of Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite, RFC 6333). It targets network architectures that use point-to-point tunnels between the access device and an access gateway built to serve large numbers of devices. The RFC names Mobile IPv6, Proxy Mobile IPv6 and GPRS Tunnelling Protocol (GTP) in mobile networks, and PPP or point-to-point VLANs in broadband networks, as examples.

DS-Lite carries IPv4 traffic in IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels from the customer network to an Address Family Transition Router (AFTR), so the inner IPv4 address does not matter for routing and private addresses can be shared between customer sites. GI-DS-Lite keeps that sharing of public IPv4 addresses, but instead of starting a new tunnel on the access device, it logically extends the existing access tunnel past the access gateway toward the AFTR.

The RFC lists the benefits: overlapping IPv4 addresses in the access network are supported, no change is needed to the access device or the access architecture, and no extra tunneling overhead is added in the access network.
sections.eli5: Homes already have a road to the local depot. Instead of paving a second road from each home to the far-away sorting office, the depot forwards the parcels and labels each one with whose it is.

sections.title: The Reference Architecture
sections.content:
Access devices (AD) connect to the access gateway (AG) over access tunnels, or over point-to-point links. How the devices get their IPv4 configuration depends on the access architecture and is outside the scope of the RFC. The access gateway and the AFTR are joined by a softwire, which is identified by a softwire identifier (SWID). The SWID need not be globally unique, and its form depends on the tunnel technology.

A Context Identifier (CID) multiplexes the flows of the individual access devices onto the softwire. The combination of CID and SWID must be unique between the access gateway and the AFTR. The CID is typically 32 bits wide and is assigned by the access gateway, taken from a local or remote repository such as an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) server. Local policy on the access gateway decides which part of an access device's traffic is tunneled to the AFTR.

The AFTR combines softwire termination with IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT. Its address is configured on the access gateway and is IPv6 or IPv4 depending on the network between them. The relationship is not 1:1: M access gateways can be connected to N AFTRs, and an AFTR may or may not be co-located with an access gateway.
sections.eli5: Each home's parcels go to the depot. The depot puts a numbered sticker on each one and sends them in a shared truck to the sorting office, which reads the sticker to know whose parcel it is.

sections.title: How the AFTR and Gateway Handle Packets
sections.content:
The AFTR builds its NAT bindings with the CID and SWID included. When it creates an IPv4-to-IPv4 binding for a flow arriving over the softwire, it SHOULD associate the CID with that binding and use the CID and SWID together as the unique identifier. For traffic going back toward the device, it SHOULD take the CID from the binding. With GRE, that means adding the CID to the GRE Key and Sequence Number extension. On any packet from the softwire it SHOULD read the CID and use it for the NAT lookup.

The NAT binding itself can be chosen by the AFTR from a local address pool, configured per binding (through a NAT control protocol or by hand), or derived from the CID. As an example, a 32-bit CID could map 1:1 to an external IPv4 address.

The access gateway looks up the CID for an access device when it receives an IPv4 packet from it, and uses the CID in packets coming from the softwire to choose where to forward them. When encapsulating, the gateway and AFTR SHOULD use the inner packet's DSCP to derive the DSCP of the softwire (or the MPLS Traffic-Class field).
sections.eli5: When a parcel comes in, the sorting office notes the sticker number next to the return address it made up. When a reply comes back, it looks up that sticker and sends it down the right branch.

sections.title: Softwire Management
sections.content:
The softwire between the access gateway and the AFTR MAY be created at system startup or established dynamically on demand. Which Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanisms watch its health, such as ICMP, Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) or LSP ping, is deployment dependent.

The peers MAY be provisioned to enforce policy, for example which protocol types or what share of traffic gets tunneled. The RFC leaves the details out of scope. They SHOULD use the correct path MTU for the tunnel path, either configured statically when the softwire is created or found dynamically with path MTU discovery. A gateway and an AFTR can also have several softwires between them, for example to separate address domains or to share load.
sections.eli5: The shared truck route can be set up in advance or when needed. The two offices check it is still working, and make sure parcels are not too big for the truck.

sections.title: Softwire Embodiments
sections.content:
The softwire can use GRE encapsulation with the GRE Key extension, MPLS VPNs, or plain IP-in-IP encapsulation. What the SWID and CID are depends on the choice:

  • GRE with GRE Key: the SWID is the GRE tunnel identifier and the CID is the GRE Key for the access device.
  • MPLS VPN: the SWID identifies the VPN and the device's IPv4 address is the CID, so it must be unique within the VPN.
  • IPv4/IPv6-in-MPLS: the SWID is the top MPLS label; the CID may be the next label, or the device's IP address.
  • IPv4-in-IPv4: the SWID is the outer IPv4 source address and the device's IPv4 address is the CID, which must be unique for that outer address.
  • IPv4-in-IPv6: the SWID is the outer IPv6 source address. With the device's IPv4 address as CID it must be unique. With the IPv6 Flow Label as CID, addresses may overlap, but the flow label is 20 bits wide, shorter than the recommended 32-bit CID, so large deployments may need extra scaling thought. The flow label should also be randomized enough to avoid interfering with uses such as Equal Cost Multipath.

A table in the RFC shows which modes support unique, overlapping or identical device addresses, and which network types (IPv4-only, IPv6-only, dual-stack or MPLS) they run over.
sections.eli5: There are several kinds of truck and labelling schemes. Some need every house to have a different number, and others let two houses share a number because the sticker tells them apart.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a packet arrives with the wrong CID, it is associated with the wrong access device, so the gateway and AFTR must carry each packet with the CID of the device it belongs to. The CID is not carried from the access device, so one device cannot claim another's CID.

An on-path attacker between the gateway and the AFTR could change the CID in a packet. The RFC says this threat is no different from an on-path attacker modifying the source or destination address of an IP packet, and that it can be prevented with IPsec with integrity protection between the gateway and the AFTR. The specification adds no new security considerations beyond those of DS-Lite (RFC 6333) and of the access architecture in use, such as Proxy Mobile IPv6.
sections.eli5: If someone swapped the stickers on the truck, parcels would go to the wrong house. A tamper-proof seal on the truck stops that.

sections.title: Call Flow and Deployment Examples
sections.content:
Appendix A gives an example of connectivity establishment. The gateway receives a request to create an access tunnel endpoint, authenticates and authorizes it, and learns from local policy or the AAA/Policy system that IPv4 service should use GI-DS-Lite. It creates the tunnel endpoint, optionally opens a control session with the AFTR (for accounting or NAT configuration, for example with the Diameter NAT Control Application), allocates a unique CID, and finally completes tunnel setup with the device, which may include assigning it an IPv4 address.

The appendix also maps the generic design to real architectures. With Dual-Stack Mobile IPv6 the home agent implements the access gateway function. With Proxy Mobile IPv6 the local mobility anchor does. In GTP-based networks the PDN-GW or GGSN does.
sections.eli5: When a new home connects, the depot checks who they are, picks a sticker number for them, and then finishes setting up their road.
